摘要导读原始字段 · 非全文

BACKGROUND: Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) associates with disease severity in pulmonary hypertension (PH). However, prior studies focused on Group 1 disease; it is unknown whether DHEA-S associates with PH severity in other etiologies. It also remains unclear if DHEA-S associations with PH severity differ by sex or menopausal status. RESEARCH QUESTION: Do associations between DHEA-S and measures of PH severity differ by PH etiology, sex, or menopausal status? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: We analyzed data from PVDOMICS, including 85 healthy controls and 710 participants with PH. Venous plasma DHEA-S levels were measured by ultraperformance liquid chromatography mass spectrometry. Multivariable regression models were used to examine associations between DHEA-S levels and invasive hemodynamics, right ventricular (RV) systolic function, and six-minute walk distance (6MWD). Analyses were stratified by sex and WSPH group, with exploratory stratification by menopausal status among subjects with Group 1 PH. RESULTS: DHEA-S levels were lower in all WSPH Groups compared with controls (adjusted p<0.01 for all). Associations between DHEA-S levels and PH severity metrics appeared most prominent in females with Group 1 PH. A doubling of DHEA-S was associated with a 2.8 mmHg (95% CI 1.6-4.1) lower mean pulmonary artery pressure, 3.2% (95% CI 2.0-4.4%) higher RV ejection fraction, and 22m (95% CI 11-33) farther 6MWD (all p<0.01). Higher DHEA-S associated with better RV function, but not pulmonary hemodynamics or 6MWD in females with Group 2 PH and males with Group 3 PH. In Group 1 PH, associations between DHEA-S and measures of PH severity appeared stronger in post-menopausal compared with premenopausal females. INTERPRETATION: Lower DHEA-S is a consistent feature across PH etiologies, but its association with disease severity appeared most pronounced in females with Group 1 PH. Modulation of DHEA-S levels or the pathways governing its regulation may represent a therapeutic target in PH, warranting further mechanistic study.

摘要导读原始字段 · 非全文

RESEARCH QUESTION: The 6-minute walk test (6MWT) is a fundamental instrument in the clinical management of COPD patients, yet the prognostic value of specific physiological parameters during the recovery phase remains underexplored. This study aimed to determine whether the recovery time of oxygen saturation (SpO2-RT) following a 6MWT is associated with long-term prognosis (death and hospitalizations) in a cohort of patients with COPD. STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: In this prospective observational cohort, 512 consecutive patients were recruited through the Galdakao University Hospital Respiratory Service and underwent pulmonary function and quadriceps strength assessments, multisensor accelerometry, and a 6MWT. Desaturation was defined as a ≥3% decrease in SpO2 from baseline during the 6MWT; SpO2-RT was the time from test completion until SpO2 returned to baseline. RESULTS: Of the 512 enrolled patients 25% were female. Those who experienced oxygen desaturation during the 6MWT exhibited significantly worse pulmonary function (FEV1%, RV%, IC/TLC and DLCO%) (p <.0001), higher fibrinogen levels (p =.01), lower quadriceps strength (p =.02), reduced PA (p <.0001), and a shorter distance walked (p <.0001). Within the desaturation sub-cohort, differences were analysed based on a SpO2-RT cut-off ≥ 80 seconds. Patients with a prolonged SpO2-RT exhibited more severe pulmonary function impairment (p values ranging from .02 to <.0001), significantly lower PA (p =.001), and shorter distance 6MWT (p <.0001). During the 3-year follow-up increased SpO2-RT was associated with increased mortality (p =.03) and hospitalizations (p =.0003). In the adjusted analyses, prolonged SpO2-RT was associated with an approximately twofold higher risk of both hospitalization (p = .02) and mortality (p =.04). INTERPRETATION: A prolonged SpO2-RT ≥ 80 identifies a COPD phenotype characterized by diminished respiratory reserve and an increased risk of subsequent exacerbation-related hospitalizations and all-cause mortality. SpO2-RT is a simple, accessible metric that enhances the prognostic utility of the standard 6MWT.
